overview: This is a broad category of farming communities, not one civilization. The imported 1500 BCE to 1530 CE outline extends as far as Somalia and omits several West African places discussed here. It is unsuitable as a cultural boundary. The named examples below show different regional histories of growing grain, preparing food and managing uncertainty.

periods.title: Early regional farming traditions
periods.summary: Nok communities in central Nigeria cultivated pearl millet within a much wider diversity of West African food-producing societies.

periods.title: Different crops and landscapes
periods.summary: Agriculture developed through varied local combinations of crops, livestock and other livelihoods.

periods.title: Diversifying harvests at Sadia
periods.summary: Farmers added or increased several cereals rather than depending only on pearl millet.

periods.title: Established agricultural systems
periods.summary: By around 1500, varied farming systems supported communities across West Africa.

sections.title: Grain, pots and places to keep the harvest

items.text: The story begins before this map window. In northern Mali, prehistoric potters mixed plant material into clay, leaving grain and chaff impressions after firing. Researchers can examine those tiny spaces to distinguish wild pearl millet from domesticated forms. A broken cooking pot can preserve evidence of crops that vanished long ago.

Domesticated pearl millet gradually developed useful traits, including heads that retained grain rather than scattering it naturally, paired spikelets and larger grains. Researchers track these changes through the impressions and charred remains. Keeping grain attached made harvesting more effective, while generations of cultivation changed the plant itself.

Dhar Néma in southeastern Mauritania, outside this imported outline, preserves a long history of farming and metalworking. At Bou Khzama II, low platforms of sandstone and quartzite cobbles resemble granary foundations in later regional communities. Archaeologists suggest a storage function; the grain bins themselves have not survived intact.

The same survey found grinding basins beside other structures, and groups of upright schist slabs that may have supported a different activity, such as drying crops. Preparing and storing food involved more than planting a field: the harvest needed processing and protection before it could become dinner.

sections.title: Meals and gatherings in central Nigeria

items.text: A study of fifty Nok sites examined more than 11,000 preserved plant remains. Pearl millet dominated, but cowpeas and fruits also occurred. Small burnt seeds reveal another side of the society famous for terracotta sculpture: feeding people required knowledgeable plant use as well as artistic skill.

The Nok millet samples contained grain but no processing chaff, even after researchers checked very fine sieve fractions. They propose that cleaned grain was brought to some ritual sites for communal consumption, perhaps feasting. The absence of the untidy bits of a crop can be a clue to where preparation happened.

Chemical analysis of Nok pottery also found beeswax, probably connected with collecting and processing honey. Some traces come from around 1500 BCE. Honey would have offered welcome sweetness, although the exact recipes are unknown. The evidence gives us a glimpse of food gathering alongside cereal farming.

sections.title: A varied menu across West Africa

items.text: At Sadia in present-day Mali, outside this outline, occupation lasted roughly from 750 to 1300 CE. Pearl millet was the main crop, but from the tenth century the evidence includes more kinds of grain, including sorghum, African rice and fonio. Researchers interpret diversification as one way of reducing the danger of a failed staple harvest.

Sadia’s plant remains also include baobab, marula, jujube, shea and African grape fruits. The dinner landscape therefore extended beyond grain fields into useful trees. These finds document collection and consumption; they do not by themselves tell us whether every tree was planted, protected or simply encountered while gathering.

Around 1500, descriptions of the West African rice coast show farmers using different heights in the landscape: wet ground, intermediate slopes and uplands. Rice plots ripened at different times, spreading the harvesting work. Careful knowledge of water and terrain could organize a farming calendar as effectively as a written timetable.

sections.title: A written celebration of useful work

items.text: A much later manuscript preserved in Timbuktu’s Mamma Haidara library discusses the social value of crafts, trades and agriculture. Its anonymous author presents useful work as a source of dignity. The surviving copy is catalogued only broadly between 1500 and 1900, so it cannot be dated precisely to this map’s final decades.

Written language sample: “فضل الحرث والزرع” means “the merits of tillage and planting.” These Arabic words appear in the red opening heading of that manuscript. This is a normalized transcription of a specific surviving page, not the language of all West African farmers or evidence that the much earlier farming communities used Arabic.

ending.text: Cereal farming did not end in 1530. Communities continued to adapt their crops, labor and landscapes as trade and political power changed. The imported endpoint closes a map category, not the history of West African agriculture.
